transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. As you know, the battery-storage installation for our distribution campus is on this month's capital-planning agenda. The proposal is a $6,000,000 purchase where we'd own the equipment outright. Before I make an approval decision, I'd like to hear from each of you -- FP&A, tax, treasury, and legal -- on anything relevant you've found regarding this project. Who would like to start?
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: I completed the project cash-flow model this morning. At our required return hurdle, the economically approvable purchase price is $4,800,000. The proposed $6,000,000 purchase price does not pass the model's hurdle. I have not yet attached the completed model to the investment-review file, but I'm sharing these findings now so they're on the record before Maya's decision.
transcript.speaker: A2

transcript.text: I received a tax memorandum this week confirming that the applicable 30% investment credit is available only when the company owns the storage equipment; a lease would make the credit unavailable. I have not yet circulated the memorandum to the planning team, but I'm sharing it now so it's on the record before Maya's decision. This is relevant because the current proposal has us owning the equipment, which would allow us to capture the credit, but if anyone is considering a lease alternative to address the pricing concern Jonas just raised, that credit would be lost.
transcript.speaker: A3

transcript.text: I need to share something from treasury regarding funding. In today's rolling cash forecast, I confirmed that only $2,000,000 can be deployed without breaching our operating-liquidity floor. The remaining $2,800,000 can be funded through an available five-year term-loan facility. I have not yet updated the funding worksheet, but I'm sharing this now so it's on the record before Maya's decision. This is relevant because the proposed $6,000,000 purchase price cannot be fully funded from cash on hand without compromising our liquidity position.
transcript.speaker: A4

transcript.text: I need to share something from legal regarding the utility interconnection agreement I reviewed this week. Energization of the battery-storage system requires a $400,000 performance bond and a signed commissioning certificate before the system can be placed in service. I have not yet added these conditions to the draft approval, but I'm sharing this now so they're on the record before Maya's decision. This is relevant because the $400,000 performance bond represents an additional cost and obligation beyond the $6,000,000 purchase price, and the commissioning certificate requirement means we cannot assume the system will be operational immediately upon purchase -- it must pass commissioning first.
transcript.speaker: A5
